Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 72, verse 1:

﴿Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened﴾. The story of these jinn who listened to the Qur'an from the Prophet (ﷺ) and embraced Islam has already been mentioned in (surah) al-Ahqaf [46:29]. ﴿And they said: Indeed we have heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾. That is, some of them said to others. And ʿajaban (wondrous) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as a description for the sake of emphasis, because ʿajab is the verbal noun of your saying ʿajibtu ʿajaban (I was amazed, with amazement). It has also been said that it is on the omission of a modifier, its estimated meaning being dha ʿajab (possessing wonder).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 72, verse 3–4:

﴿And that He, exalted is He, is the majesty (jadd) of our Lord﴾. Jadd (ـ) of Allah means His majesty and His greatness. It has also been said that its meaning derives from your saying: "So-and-so is majdud," meaning he has become wealthy (istaghna). In this place it is read with the hamza of "anna" open (fatha), and Nafi' read it with a kasra; likewise in what follows, up to His saying: ﴿And that among us are the Muslims﴾. As for the kasra, it is either a resumption (isti'naf) or a conjunction (atf) upon "innā sami'nā" (indeed we heard), but the kasra occurs in the object of the verb "qala" (say), so it is conjoined to it as part of the speech of the jinn. As for the fatha, it has been said that it is conjoined to His saying: "innahu istama'a nafar" (indeed a group of them listened), and this is an error in terms of meaning, because His saying "istama'a nafar" stands in the position of the object of "uhiya" (it was revealed), so it would follow that the conjoined element is part of what was revealed and not part of the speech of the jinn. It has also been said that it is conjoined to the pronoun in the genitive in His saying: "amanna bihi" (we believed in it), and this is weak, because a pronoun in the genitive cannot be conjoined to except by repeating the governing preposition.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is conjoined to the position (mahall) of the prepositional phrase in "amanna bihi," as if he said: "We affirmed it and we affirmed that He, exalted is He, is the majesty of our Lord," and likewise what follows it. There is no disagreement about the fatha in three places: "annahu istama'a" (indeed He listened), "wa-an law istaqamu" (and that if they had remained upright), and "wa-anna al-masajida lillah" (and that the mosques are for Allah), because these are among what was revealed and not part of the speech of the jinn. ﴿And that it was that the foolish one among us used to say about Allah an outrageous lie (shatat)﴾. This is part of the speech of the jinn. Their foolish one (safih) is their father Iblis. It has also been said that it is a generic noun for every foolish one among them, and Ibn 'Atiyyah chose this view. Shatat means transgression and exceeding the bounds.

"And we had thought that men and jinn would never speak a lie against Allah."

That is, we had thought that the statements which men and jinn used to make about Allah were true and not lies, because we thought that no one would lie against Allah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 72, verse 6:

﴿And that there were men among mankind who used to seek refuge with men among the jinn﴾ Tafsir: This is what has been related: when one of the Arabs would arrive at a valley, he would call out at the top of his voice: "O Master (ʿAziz) of this valley, I seek refuge with you from the foolish ones who are under your obedience," believing that the jinn who dwell in the valley would protect him. ﴿So they increased them in distress﴾ The subject pronoun refers to the jinn, and the object pronoun refers to mankind. The meaning: the jinn increased mankind in misguidance and sin when they sought refuge with them; or they increased them in fear, since they saw the weakness of their minds. It has also been said: the subject pronoun refers to mankind, and the object pronoun refers to the jinn. The meaning: mankind increased the jinn in arrogance and tyranny when they sought refuge with them, until the jinn would say: "I am the lord of the jinn and mankind."

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 72, verse 7:

﴿And that they thought, as you thought, that Allah would never resurrect anyone.﴾ The pronoun in "ظنوا" (thought) refers to the disbelievers among mankind, while "ظننتم" (you thought) is an address from the jinn to one another. The meaning, then, is that the disbelievers among mankind and among the jinn both thought that Allah would never send anyone (as a messenger), and "al-ba'th" (resurrection, here: sending) here may be intended to mean either the sending of messengers or the raising of people from their graves.

And that we sought (to reach) the heaven, but found it filled with a strong guard and meteors.

This is a report of what happened at the time of the Prophet's (ﷺ) mission: the jinn were prevented from eavesdropping on the heaven and were pelted. "Lams" (touching) means "mass" (touching), and it is used here metaphorically for seeking (ṭalab). "Ḥaras" (guard) is a singular noun meaning "ḥurrās" (guards), like "khadam" (servants) meaning "khuddām" (attendants). For this reason it is described by "shadīd" (strong), which is singular. It may also mean the guarding angels, or the guarding stars. "Shuhub" (meteors) is repeated because the wording differs.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 72, verse 9:

﴿And we used to sit in it on certain seats to listen (for news)﴾. Al-maqa'id is the plural of maq'ad (seat). The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained the manner of the jinn's sitting: they were arranged one above another, so that whenever the uppermost was burned, the one beneath him would rise up in his place. They would snatch a word and convey it to the soothsayers (kahan, diviners), adding to it of their own. Then the soothsayers would add a hundred lies to the word. ﴿But whoever listens now will find for himself a watching flame lying in wait﴾. Al-rasad is a collective noun for al-raqib (watcher), like hurras for haris (guard). Ibn 'Atiyya said: it is a verbal noun (masdar) used as a descriptive, and its meaning is "awaiting." Some of them said: the pelting of the jinn with stars only occurred after the mission (mab'ath) of the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari chose that it was a little before the mission, then it increased after the mission and became frequent until the jinn were entirely prevented from eavesdropping. The evidence that it existed before the mission is the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to his companions when he saw a star shooting across the sky: "What used you to say about this in the Jahiliyyah?" They said: "We used to say that a king had been born or a king had died." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The matter is not as such." Then he described the jinn's eavesdropping, and the poets of the Jahiliyyah mentioned that in their poetry.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 72, verse 10–13:

﴿And indeed, we do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth﴾ — the verse: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: its meaning is: we do not know whether people will believe in this Prophet and be guided, or whether they will disbelieve in him and evil will befall them? Al-Zamakhshari said: its meaning is: we do not know whether Allah intended for the people of the earth good or evil, a punishment or a mercy, abandonment or divine success? ﴿And indeed among us are the righteous, and among us are those below that﴾ — i.e., among us are a people below that, so the qualified noun is omitted, and by it he meant those whose righteousness is not complete, or those who have no righteousness at all, for dūn (دون, "below, other than") can mean "less" or "other than." ﴿We were paths, divided in ways﴾ — ṭarāʾiq (طرائق) means schools of thought, ways and courses and the like, and qidad (قدد) means divergent, and it is the plural of qidda (قدة). This is an explanation of the division mentioned before, and it is by omitting a noun: i.e., we were people of different paths. ﴿And indeed we thought that we would never escape Allah in the earth﴾ — ẓann (الظن) here means knowledge. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this is a report from them about their state after their faith, and it is possible that they held this belief before their Islam. ﴿When we heard the guidance﴾ — they mean the Qur'an. ﴿So he does not fear any diminution or any burden﴾ — bakhs (البخس) is deficiency and injustice, and rahaq (الرهق) is bearing what cannot be endured. Ibn ʿAbbas said: bakhs is the reduction of good deeds, and rahaq is the increase in bad deeds.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 72, verse 14–17:

﴿And among us are the unjust (al-qasitun)﴾. He means the wrongdoers. It is said: "qasata al-rajul" when a man acts unjustly, and "aqsata" with the alif when he acts justly.

Here ends what Allah related of the speech of the jinn. As for His saying: ﴿Then whoever has submitted, those have sought out the right course﴾, it may be part of their speech, or it may be the beginning of Allah's own speech, and this is what Ibn 'Atiyyah (Ibn ʿAṭiyyah) chose. As for His saying: ﴿And if they had remained upright on the way﴾, it is by agreement the speech of Allah, and not of theirs.

﴿Taḥarraw﴾: that is, they intended the right course (rushd). ﴿And if they had remained upright on the way, We would have given them abundant water (ma'an ghadaqan)﴾. Ghadaq means abundant. This is a metaphor for the expansion of provision. The "way" (ṭarīqah) is the way of Islam and obedience to Allah, so the meaning is: if they had remained steadfast upon it, Allah would have expanded their provision. This is like His saying: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of Allah, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 96]. It was also said: the "way" is the way of disbelief, and the meaning on this view is: if they had remained steadfast in disbelief, Allah would have expanded their worldly possessions as a gradual trap (istidraj). The words ﴿that We may test them therein﴾ support this. The first view is more apparent. The pronoun in ﴿istaqamu﴾ may refer to the Muslims or to the unjust mentioned, or to all the jinn, or to the jinn who heard the Prophet (ﷺ), or to all creation. ﴿That We may test them therein﴾: if the way is faith and obedience, then the meaning of "fitnah" is testing: whether they will submit or not. If the way is disbelief, then the meaning of "fitnah" is misguidance and gradual trap. ﴿He will make him enter a painful punishment (adhaban saʿadan)﴾: the meaning of "nuslikuhu" is that We cause him to enter. "Ṣaʿad" means severe hardship; it is a verbal noun from "ṣaʿida yaṣʿadu," and it is described by the verbal noun for emphasis. It is said: "fulan fi ṣaʿad," meaning he is in hardship. It was also said: "ṣaʿadan" is a mountain in Hell.

﴿And indeed, the mosques belong to Allah﴾. He meant mosques in the absolute sense, and they are the houses of worship of Allah. It is related that the verse was revealed concerning the domination of the Ka'bah by the Quraysh. It was also said that he meant the body parts upon which one prostrates (al-a'da' al-lati yasjudu 'alayha), whose singular is masjad with a fatha on the jim, but this is far-fetched. The conjunction "and that the mosques belong to Allah" is coordinated with "it has been revealed to me that he listened" (the earlier verse wording). Al-Khalil said: the meaning of the verse is: "Because the mosques belong to Allah, do not call upon anyone along with Allah," i.e., for this reason, do not worship other than Allah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 72, verse 19:

﴿And when the servant of Allah stood up calling upon Him﴾: "The servant of Allah" here is Muhammad (ﷺ). He is described with servitude (ʿubudiyya) as a mark of distinction, nearness, and honour.

Al-Zamakhshari said: He named him here "the servant of Allah" and did not say "the Messenger" or "the Prophet," because this description occurs in the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) himself, since it is something that was revealed to him, so he (ﷺ) mentioned himself in the manner that humility and self-abasement require. But what he said is far-fetched, and it is only possible on the reading "lamma qama" with the hamza opened, so that it is a conjunction with "uhiya ilayya annahu istamaʿa" (it was revealed to me that it listened). As for the reading with the hamza kasra, on the basis of a new sentence (istiʾnaf), it is then a report from Allah, or part of the speech of the jinn, and what he said is invalidated.

﴿They almost became, against him, a crowd﴾: al-libad (لبد) means groups, and its singular is libda (لبدة). The pronoun in "kadu" (كادوا) may refer to the disbelievers among mankind, meaning they nearly gathered together to oppose him and nullify his affair; or it may refer to the jinn who listened, meaning they nearly gathered around him to listen to the Qur'an and seek its blessing.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 72, verse 22–24:

﴿مُلْتَحَداً﴾ means a refuge, a place of shelter. ﴿إِلاَّ بَلاَغاً﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿مُلْتَحَداً﴾, meaning: I will not find a refuge except the conveying of the message. It may also be an exceptive (istithna') that is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning "but only the conveying". ﴿مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ﴾: al-Zamakhshari said: this prepositional phrase (al-jar wa-al-majrur) is not a complement (silah) of "al-balagh"; rather it has the sense of "balaghan ka'inan min Allah" (a conveyance that comes from God). In my view, it may also be connected to "balaghan", and the meaning would be "a conveyance from God". ﴿وَرِسَالاَتِهِ﴾: al-Zamakhshari said: it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "balaghan", as if he said: "except the conveying and the messages". It may also be that "wa-risalatihi" is conjoined to the name of God (ism Allah).

﴿وَمَن يَعْصِ ٱللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ فَإِنَّ لَهُ نَارَ جَهَنَّمَ خَالِدِينَ فِيهَآ أَبَداً﴾ "Khalidin" is in the plural on the meaning of "man" (whoever), since "man" carries the sense of the plural. The verse concerns the disbelievers. The Mu'tazilah applied it to disobedient believers, because their doctrine is that such people abide eternally in the Fire. There are two proofs that it concerns the disbelievers: first, that the surah is Meccan, and Meccan surahs are addressed primarily to the disbelievers; second, that what precedes and what follows it indicates that the intended meaning is the disbelievers. ﴿حَتَّىٰ إِذَا رَأَوْاْ مَا يُوعَدُونَ﴾: "hatta" is connected to his saying "yakununa 'alayhi libadan" (they would be crowding around him), and it is made the endpoint (ghayah) of that. The meaning is: they persist in disbelief and gather together against him until, when they see what they are promised. Al-Zamakhshari said this. He also said: it may be connected to an omitted element (mahdhuf) that indicates the meaning, as if it were said: "They will continue in what they are upon of disbelief until, when they see what they are promised." This is more apparent.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 72, verses 25–28:

﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will set for it a long term.﴾ Here "in" (إن) is negative. The meaning is: say, "I do not know whether what you are promised is near or far." He expressed its distance by his saying, "or whether my Lord will set for it a long term." By "what you are promised" is meant their being killed on the day of Badr, or the Day of Resurrection.

﴿He does not reveal His unseen to anyone, except to one whom He has approved﴾: that is, He does not let anyone have knowledge of the unseen, ﴿except one whom He has approved﴾, and these are the messengers, for He informs them of whatever of that He wills. The "min" (مِن) in His saying ﴿of a messenger﴾ is for specifying the genus, not for partitioning. The "messengers" here may be understood as messengers from among the angels, and this is how Ibn 'Atiyya interpreted it, or as messengers from among the children of Adam, and this is how al-Zamakhshari interpreted it. It has been used as evidence to deny the miracles (karamat) of the saints who claim unveilings (mukashafat), since God has restricted the access to the unseen to the messengers and no others. It also contains proof for invalidating soothsaying (kahana), astrology (tanjim), and all other means by which their practitioners claim access to the unseen, since they are not among the messengers.

﴿For He makes a guard march before him and behind him﴾: the meaning is that God makes, before the messengers and behind them, angels who serve as a guard (rasad), protecting them from the devils. We have already mentioned "rasad" in this surah. Some of them said: God has sent no messenger without angels accompanying him to guard him until he conveys the message of his Lord.

﴿That He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord.﴾ Regarding the subject of "ya'lam" (that He may know) there are three opinions. The first: that God may know that the messengers have conveyed the messages of their Lord, that is, He knows it as existing, although He had known it before it occurred. The second: that Muhammad may know that the watching angels have conveyed the messages of their Lord. The third: that the disbelievers may know that the messengers have conveyed the message. The first is the most apparent. The pronoun in "they have conveyed" (أبلغوا) is plural in "their Lord" (ربهم) in consideration of meaning, because "one whom He has approved" among the messengers refers to a group.

﴿And He encompasses what is with them﴾: that is, God encompasses what the messengers have of knowledge and laws. This clause is conjoined to His saying "that He may know," because its meaning is that He has known. Ibn 'Atiyya said this. It is also possible that this clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿And He has counted everything in number﴾: this is a general statement covering all things. "'Adadan" (عَدَداً) is in the accusative either as a circumstantial accusative (hal), or as a specification (tamyiz), or as a verbal noun (masdar) from the sense of "ahsa."
